title: Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story
full_review:
With a running time just north of 90 minutes, "Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story" (20th Century Fox) is about an hour and a half too long.

Full of forced, crass humor, this doggedly dreadful movie tries to capitalize on viewers' childhood memories of gym-class trauma, resulting in an experience about as enjoyable as getting drilled in the kisser with a rubber ball hurled by some snotty seventh-grade sadist.

Vince Vaughn stars as Peter LaFleur, a rakish underachiever and proprietor of a fleabag gym called Average Joe's. The rundown joint serves as a watering hole for a motley bunch of social rejects, including a self-styled pirate (Alan Tudyk) and a scrawny nerd (Justin Long) whose most common experience with a gym locker is getting stuffed into one.

To make a dumb story short, LaFleur's nonexistent bookkeeping and kindhearted habit of letting his friends slide on paying membership dues leaves him $50,000 in arrears.

Licking his faux tan chops at the prospect of bulldozing Average Joe's and turning it into a parking lot is White Goodman (Ben Stiller), LaFleur's cross-street rival, a narcissistic fitness freak and owner of the state-of-the-art Globo Gym where the sales pitch is, "We're better than you and you know it."

With their beloved gym facing closure, the scrappy misfits come up with the idea of forming a dodgeball team with their hopes set on winning a high-stakes tournament in Las Vegas with a cash prize of $50,000.

Predictably, the lovable losers prevail against all odds and make it to the final round. But in order to go the distance they must face Globo Gym's Purple Cobras -- a team of steroid-enhanced all-stars captained by Goodman -- in a winner-takes-all showdown.

Christine Taylor plays Kate Veatch, an attorney sent by the bank to facilitate the foreclosing of Average Joe's, but who winds up being their team's secret weapon. Rip Torn plays the crotchety, wheelchair-bound Patches O'Houlihan, a legendary dodgeball icon who pilots LaFleur's sad-sack squad from geekdom to greatness and helps them connect with their inner champion.

O'Houlihan teaches them that the key to success in the sport can be distilled down to the five-point mantra, "Dodge, duck, dip, dive and dodge" -- driving home the importance of each by firing wrenches at them, "If you can dodge a wrench, you can dodge a ball."

Moviegoers would be well advised to add "dash" to that list -- as in away from any theater playing this clunker.

As directed by Rawson Marshall Thurber, "Dodgeball" follows the well-worn David-vs.-Goliath formula of such comedies as "The Bad News Bears," but its love-yourself-for-who-you-are message is weighed down by the film's preponderance of puerility including jokes about lesbianism, penile pumps, S&M leatherwear and, of course, running sight gags of people getting smashed in the face -- or considerably lower -- with spherical projectiles. A few chuckles are provided by a peppering of campy cameos including David Hasselhoff and William Shatner.

As viewers are reminded throughout the film, Average Joe's team motto is "aim low" -- a slogan which could just as easily be applied to the comedic aspirations of this movie.

Due to recurring crude and sexual language and humor, an instance of rough language and profanity and same-sex kissing, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
